html:
The Virgin Lands campaign was the plan of the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev to grow wheat on the untouched grasslands of northern Kazakhstan and western Siberia, launched in 1954 to ease food shortages in the Soviet Union.

Hundreds of thousands of young volunteers, many from Russia and Ukraine, were sent east by train. They lived at first in tents and ploughed millions of hectares of steppe in a few years. Leonid Brezhnev, later Soviet leader, helped run the campaign as a party chief in Kazakhstan.

What happened:

  • The first harvests, above all in 1956, were huge, and the campaign was hailed as a triumph.
  • Then yields fell. Repeated wheat crops wore out the thin soils, and droughts hit.
  • In the early 1960s dust storms blew away topsoil over large areas, an ecological disaster for the Kazakh steppe.
  • The Soviet Union still had to buy grain abroad from 1963.

The campaign changed the people of Kazakhstan. So many settlers arrived that Kazakhs, already reduced by the famine of the 1930s, were a minority in their own republic. The town of Akmolinsk was renamed Tselinograd, "Virgin Lands City", in 1961. Under other names it later became the capital of independent Kazakhstan.

It belongs with other big Soviet schemes to remake nature, like the irrigation of the Hungry Steppe for cotton, that brought short gains and long damage under Soviet rule.
sum: The Virgin Lands campaign was the plan of the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev to grow wheat on the untouched grasslands of northern Kazakhstan and western Siberia, launched in 1954 to ease food shortages in the Soviet Union.
